buildings.palace: Seats of power, from the walled compounds of early kings to modern presidential residences, have long anchored the reach of the state. The Palace marks your capital: the city that holds it suffers no corruption, and distance from it drives [corruption](pedia:concepts/corruption) in every other city. A capital cannot be turned by propaganda or lost to a culture flip. Rebuild it elsewhere only if the heart of your empire has moved, since the old Palace is removed.
buildings.barracks: Permanent garrisons with drill grounds let ancient states turn farmers into trained soldiers. Land units built in a city with Barracks start as veterans, and wounded land units resting there recover all their hit points in a single turn. Build them in the few cities that train your armies rather than everywhere, since the upkeep adds up.
buildings.granary: Storing grain against lean years was one of the first tasks of organised government. When a city with a Granary grows, its food box starts half full instead of empty, so the next citizen arrives much sooner. It pays off in food-rich cities you want to grow quickly or that keep producing settlers and workers.
buildings.temple: Shrines and temples gave early communities a shared place of worship and a calendar of festivals. A Temple makes one unhappy citizen content in its city and adds to the city's culture, helping its borders grow. It is usually the first defence against disorder once a city outgrows its born-content citizens.
buildings.marketplace: Open markets drew traders and craftsmen to every town worth the name. A Marketplace raises the city's tax and luxury output by half, and it multiplies the happiness that connected luxury resources provide. Build it in cities with strong commerce, or where several luxuries arrive and contentment is a struggle.
buildings.library: Collections of written works, from clay tablets to scrolls, preserved knowledge across generations. A Library raises the city's science output by half and adds culture. Build it first in your high-commerce cities; it is also needed before a University.
buildings.courthouse: Local courts carried the ruler's law to places far from the throne. A Courthouse halves corruption and waste in its city and makes enemy propaganda against it succeed half as often. It earns its upkeep in distant cities, or in large empires where [corruption](pedia:concepts/corruption) eats much of the commerce and shields.
buildings.walls: Stone and earthen ramparts protected towns from raiders for thousands of years. Walls add half again to the defence of units in the city against land attacks, but only while the city is still a town; larger cities rely on their own size bonus instead. They also shield the city's citizens and buildings from land [bombardment](pedia:concepts/bombard) with a defence of 8. Build them early in exposed border towns.
buildings.aqueduct: Engineered channels carried clean water over long distances to supply growing cities. An Aqueduct lets a town grow beyond the town size limit into a full city. Cities beside a river or lake already have fresh water and reach that size without one, so build it where a town stalls at the cap.
buildings.bank: Banking houses lent money, held deposits and financed trade across Renaissance Europe. A Bank adds another half to the city's tax output on top of the Marketplace it requires. Build it where commerce is high and you lean on the tax rate for income.
buildings.cathedral: Great churches took generations to raise and became the centre of medieval civic life. A Cathedral makes three unhappy citizens content in its city and adds culture; it needs a Temple first. Choose it for large cities that have outgrown what a Temple and luxuries can hold.
buildings.university: The universities of medieval Europe gathered scholars under a common charter for learning. A University adds another half to the city's science output on top of the Library it requires. Put it in your most commercial cities, where every extra beaker counts.
buildings.colosseum: Arenas staged games and spectacles that kept restless city crowds entertained. A Colosseum makes two unhappy citizens content in its city. It is a solid way to steady growing cities before Cathedrals become available, though it adds no culture of note.
buildings.factory: Mechanised workshops driven by steam and later electricity transformed how goods were made. A Factory raises the city's shield output by half, but it needs Iron and adds to the city's [pollution](pedia:concepts/pollution). Build it in your best production cities; a power plant later raises its bonus further.
buildings.manufacturingPlant: Automated assembly lines pushed industrial output to new heights. A Manufacturing Plant adds another half to the city's shields on top of the Factory it requires, at the cost of more pollution. Reserve it for core industrial cities that build wonders, spaceship parts or armies.
buildings.recyclingCenter: Recovering metal, paper and glass reduces waste and the demand for raw materials. A Recycling Center cuts the pollution caused by a city's industrial buildings by about two thirds. Build it in heavy-industry cities that keep fouling the land around them.
buildings.coalPlant: Coal-fired generators powered the first electrical grids. A Coal Plant increases the extra production a Factory provides, but it needs Coal and pollutes heavily. Only one power plant can stand in a city, so building a cleaner one later replaces it.
buildings.hydroPlant: Dams harness falling water to make electricity without burning fuel. A Hydro Plant boosts the city's Factory output like other power plants but adds no pollution. It can only be built where a river runs through the city's work area; building a different plant later replaces it.
buildings.nuclearPlant: Fission reactors produce vast amounts of power from very little fuel. A Nuclear Plant gives the biggest boost to Factory output of any power plant without polluting, but it needs Uranium and water nearby. While the city is in disorder it may melt down, killing half the population and polluting the land around it, so keep such cities content.
buildings.hospital: Modern hospitals and public health measures let crowded cities stay healthy. A Hospital removes the limit on city size, letting a city grow into a metropolis. It can only be built in a city already past town size; add it when a city reaches the size an Aqueduct allows.
buildings.researchLab: Corporate and government laboratories turned research into an organised industry. A Research Lab adds another half to the city's science on top of the University it requires, though it pollutes a little. Build it in your leading science cities in the late game.
buildings.massTransitSystem: Subways, trams and buses moved commuters without choking the streets with cars. A Mass Transit System removes the pollution caused by a city's population, leaving only what its industry produces. It needs Rubber and is worth building once large cities begin to pollute on their own.
buildings.samMissileBattery: Batteries of surface-to-air missiles were built to guard cities against bombers. The SAM Missile Battery needs Aluminum. Units defending its city against air strikes get +100%, and the city's anti-air fire is doubled, though the battery does not shoot by itself: keep [Flak](pedia:units/flak) or [Mobile SAM](pedia:units/mobileSam) units in the city. It is also required before [Strategic Missile Defense](pedia:buildings/strategicMissileDefense).
buildings.coastalFortress: Gun batteries along harbours guarded ports against enemy fleets. A Coastal Fortress strengthens the city's defenders by half against attacks from the sea and shields its citizens and buildings from naval [bombardment](pedia:concepts/bombard) with a defence of 8. It needs Iron and Saltpeter; build it in exposed ports when enemy navies threaten your coast.
buildings.solarPlant: Solar collectors turn sunlight directly into electricity. A Solar Plant boosts Factory output like other power plants without polluting and without needing a river or a resource. As with any power plant, only one can stand in a city, and building it replaces an older plant.
buildings.harbor: Sheltered harbours with quays let fishing fleets and merchants work in safety. A Harbor adds one food to every water tile the city works, makes new ships veteran, repairs damaged ships fully in port, and joins the city to the [trade](pedia:concepts/trade) network over water. It is often the best early building for a coastal city with many water tiles.
buildings.offshorePlatform: Drilling and mining rigs reached the resources beneath the sea floor. An Offshore Platform adds one shield to every water tile the city works, at the cost of extra pollution. Build it in coastal cities that have little land and lack production.
buildings.airport: Airports opened fast travel between distant cities and continents. An Airport makes new aircraft veteran, repairs aircraft fully, and lets one unit a turn be airlifted from the city to another of your cities. It pollutes a little; build it in a few hubs between which you need to move troops quickly.
buildings.policeStation: Organised police forces kept order in growing industrial cities. A Police Station cuts corruption and waste in its city and halves the unhappiness that war weariness causes there. Build it in distant cities, or wherever war weariness bites under a [Republic](pedia:governments/republic) or [Democracy](pedia:governments/democracy).
buildings.wealth: Not every workshop needs to raise a new building; sometimes the state simply sells what it makes. Choosing Wealth turns all of a city's shields into gold each turn, at a better rate once Economics is known. Use it when a city has nothing useful left to build. Wealth cannot be hurried.
buildings.pyramids: The great tombs of the Egyptian kings were among the largest structures of the ancient world. The Pyramids act as a Granary in every one of your cities on the same continent, so growing cities keep half of their food box. They suit an expansive start with many cities sharing one landmass.
buildings.hangingGardens: Legend credits a Babylonian king with terraced gardens built to remind his queen of her green homeland. The Hanging Gardens make three unhappy citizens content in their own city and one in every other city you own. They lose their effect once Steam Power is discovered.
buildings.colossus: A giant bronze statue of the sun god once stood over the harbour of Rhodes. The Colossus adds one commerce to every tile its city works that already yields commerce, making a coastal city a strong early trading centre. Its effect ends with Flight.
buildings.greatLighthouse: The lighthouse at Alexandria guided ships into port for centuries. The Great Lighthouse gives all your ships one extra movement point and lets coast-hugging vessels such as [Galleys](pedia:units/galley) cross sea tiles safely, though never ocean. It becomes obsolete with Magnetism, so it pays most for early seafaring civilizations.
buildings.greatLibrary: The library of Alexandria set out to gather a copy of every book in the known world. At the end of each turn the Great Library gives its owner any advance it could research that at least two civilizations it has met already know. It keeps a lagging civilization in step until Education makes it obsolete.
buildings.oracle: Pilgrims travelled to Delphi to hear the pronouncements of the god's priestess. The Oracle doubles the contentment provided by every Temple you own. It loses its effect with Theology, so build it early if you rely on temples to keep your cities calm.
buildings.greatWall: Successive Chinese dynasties built and rebuilt long walls along their northern frontier. The Great Wall acts as Walls in every city of yours on its continent and doubles your units' strength in combat against barbarians. It becomes obsolete with Metallurgy.
buildings.sunTzusArtOfWar: An ancient Chinese treatise on strategy is still read by commanders and managers today. Sun Tzu's Art of War acts as Barracks in every city of yours on its continent, so land units are trained as veterans and heal fully at home. Militaristic empires that fight on one landmass gain the most from it.
buildings.sistineChapel: Michelangelo spent four years painting the ceiling of the pope's chapel in Rome. The Sistine Chapel doubles the contentment provided by every Cathedral you own. Build it if your large cities depend on cathedrals to stay out of disorder.
buildings.magellansVoyage: Magellan's expedition was the first to sail around the globe, though he did not survive the journey. Magellan's Voyage gives all your ships one extra movement point. It is most valuable for naval powers and island empires that move their troops by sea.
buildings.copernicusObservatory: Copernicus argued that the Earth circles the Sun, overturning centuries of accepted astronomy. Copernicus' Observatory doubles the science produced in its own city. Place it in your best research city, ideally one that already has a Library and University.
buildings.shakespearesTheater: The Globe in London staged Shakespeare's plays to crowds from every walk of life. Shakespeare's Theater makes up to eight unhappy citizens content in its city and removes the city's size limit. It turns one large city into a metropolis that rarely riots; it must be built in a city, not a town.
buildings.leonardosWorkshop: Leonardo da Vinci filled his notebooks with machines far ahead of his time. Leonardo's Workshop halves the gold cost of upgrading your units to newer types. It saves a great deal for a large standing army that must keep pace with new technology.
buildings.jsBachsCathedral: Johann Sebastian Bach wrote hundreds of works for the church services of Leipzig. J.S. Bach's Cathedral makes two unhappy citizens content in every one of your cities on its continent. Build it on your main landmass to ease unrest across the heart of your empire.
buildings.newtonsUniversity: Newton's laws of motion and gravitation remade the science of physics. Newton's University doubles the science produced in its own city. Place it in your best research city, where it stacks with Copernicus' Observatory and the city's own science buildings.
buildings.smithsTradingCompany: Adam Smith described how markets and the division of labour create the wealth of nations. Smith's Trading Company pays the upkeep of every commercial building in your empire that costs one gold a turn, such as Marketplaces and Harbors. It frees a large treasury burden in a wide empire.
buildings.universalSuffrage: Extending the vote to every adult citizen changed what governments owed their people. Universal Suffrage halves war weariness in all your cities, on top of any Police Station. It is the natural companion of a [Republic](pedia:governments/republic) or [Democracy](pedia:governments/democracy) that has to fight long wars.
buildings.hooverDam: The great concrete dam on the Colorado River powered cities across the American Southwest. Hoover Dam acts as a Hydro Plant in every city of yours on its continent, boosting factory output without pollution. It must be built in a city with a river in its work area.
buildings.theoryOfEvolution: Darwin's account of natural selection reshaped biology and challenged long-held beliefs. The Theory of Evolution grants its builder two free advances. It is a strong pick when you are racing for a key technology or trying to catch up with a rival.
buildings.unitedNations: Founded after the Second World War, the United Nations gave its member states a shared assembly. While anyone holds the United Nations, elections for world leadership are held, and winning one brings a diplomatic [victory](pedia:concepts/victory). Build it if you have many friends among the other civilizations.
buildings.manhattanProject: A secret wartime programme produced the first atomic bombs. Once the Manhattan Project stands anywhere in the world, every civilization with the right technology may build nuclear weapons, not only its builder. It needs Uranium; think carefully before completing it, since it arms your rivals as well.
buildings.cureForCancer: Defeating cancer would rank among the greatest achievements of medicine. The Cure for Cancer makes one unhappy citizen content in every city you own, including its own. It is a steady late-game boost to contentment across a large empire.
buildings.longevity: Advances in genetics promise to extend healthy human life. With Longevity, your cities grow by two citizens instead of one whenever their food box fills, as far as their size limit allows. It speeds the growth of every city in a large empire.
buildings.setiProgram: Radio telescopes have long listened for signals from other civilizations among the stars. The SETI Program doubles the science produced in its own city. Put it in your leading research city to speed the final race through the technology tree.
buildings.heroicEpic: Epic poems celebrated the deeds of legendary warriors and kings. The Heroic Epic doubles the chance that an elite unit winning a battle brings forth a great leader. It can only be built after one of your armies has won a battle.
buildings.ironWorks: Foundries that combined iron ore and coal fed the rise of heavy industry. The Iron Works doubles its city's shield output, but it needs both Iron and Coal and pollutes heavily. Build it in the city you intend to make your industrial centre.
buildings.forbiddenPalace: The imperial palace in Beijing housed emperors and their court for five centuries. The Forbidden Palace acts as a second seat of government: corruption and waste in nearby cities are measured from it as well as from your capital. Build it at the centre of a distant group of cities.
buildings.militaryAcademy: Professional academies trained officers in strategy and command. The Military Academy lets its city build armies directly, without waiting for a great leader, within your usual army limit. It becomes available once one of your armies has won a battle.
buildings.pentagon: The headquarters of the United States military is one of the largest office buildings in the world. The Pentagon lets each of your armies hold one more unit. It can only be started once you have at least one army.
buildings.wallStreet: A narrow street in Manhattan became shorthand for the world of finance. Wall Street pays interest on a positive treasury every turn, up to a fixed maximum. It requires a Stock Exchange and rewards a civilization that keeps a large gold reserve.
buildings.apolloProgram: The programme that landed people on the Moon showed what a concentrated national effort could achieve. The Apollo Program lets your civilization build the parts of a [spaceship](pedia:concepts/spaceship). It needs Aluminum; build it early if you mean to win the space race.
buildings.strategicMissileDefense: Systems to intercept ballistic missiles have long been a goal of defence planners. Strategic Missile Defense gives a strong chance to stop any nuclear strike aimed within three tiles of one of your cities. It requires a SAM Missile Battery; build it once rivals have the bomb.
buildings.intelligenceAgency: Modern states built permanent services to gather secrets and run agents abroad. The Intelligence Agency allows spy missions such as planting a spy in a rival civilization or exposing enemy agents, and it makes every enemy mission against you less likely to succeed. Build it once espionage starts to matter.
buildings.battlefieldMedicine: Field hospitals and trained medics saved soldiers who would once have died of their wounds. Battlefield Medicine lets your units heal while they stand in enemy territory. It requires a Hospital in one of your cities and helps sustain long offensive campaigns far from home.
buildings.ssThrusters: Thrusters give a spacecraft fine control over its course during a long voyage. SS Thrusters are one of the ten parts needed to complete a [spaceship](pedia:concepts/spaceship), and they need Aluminum and your own Apollo Program. A finished part joins the ship rather than staying in the city.
buildings.ssEngine: Powerful engines must carry a colony ship out of orbit and across interstellar space. The SS Engine is one of the ten parts of a [spaceship](pedia:concepts/spaceship); it needs Aluminum and your own Apollo Program. Build it in a high-production city, since every part must be finished before launch.
buildings.ssDockingBay: Orbital docking bays let a ship be assembled piece by piece above the planet. The SS Docking Bay is one of the ten parts of a [spaceship](pedia:concepts/spaceship) and needs Aluminum and your own Apollo Program. Like every part, it joins the ship as soon as it is complete.
buildings.ssCockpit: The command module holds the crew who guide the ship through its journey. The SS Cockpit is one of the ten parts needed for a [spaceship](pedia:concepts/spaceship); it needs Aluminum and your own Apollo Program. Spread the parts across your strongest cities to finish the ship quickly.
buildings.ssFuelCells: Compact fuel cells store the energy that keeps a long voyage going. SS Fuel Cells are one of the ten parts of a [spaceship](pedia:concepts/spaceship) and need Uranium rather than Aluminum, along with your own Apollo Program. Secure a Uranium source well before you need them.
buildings.ssLifeSupportSystem: Recycling air and water is essential for keeping a crew alive far from home. The SS Life Support System is one of the ten parts of a [spaceship](pedia:concepts/spaceship); it needs Aluminum and your own Apollo Program. The ship cannot launch until every part is in place.
buildings.ssStasisChamber: Suspended animation would let colonists sleep through a journey of many years. The SS Stasis Chamber is one of the ten parts of a [spaceship](pedia:concepts/spaceship) and needs both Aluminum and Uranium, as well as your own Apollo Program. It is often the hardest part to supply.
buildings.ssStorageSupply: A colony needs tools, seed and supplies to survive its first years on a new world. The SS Storage/Supply module is one of the ten parts of a [spaceship](pedia:concepts/spaceship); it needs Aluminum and your own Apollo Program. A finished part joins the ship instead of standing in the city.
buildings.ssPlanetaryPartyLounge: Even pioneers on a voyage between the stars need somewhere to relax. The SS Planetary Party Lounge is one of the ten parts of a [spaceship](pedia:concepts/spaceship) and needs Aluminum and your own Apollo Program. The ship cannot launch without it.
buildings.ssExteriorCasing: A tough outer hull shields the ship and its passengers from radiation and debris. The SS Exterior Casing is one of the ten parts of a [spaceship](pedia:concepts/spaceship); it needs Aluminum and Rubber along with your own Apollo Program. Make sure both resources reach the city that builds it.
buildings.internet: A worldwide network of linked computers changed how knowledge is shared and stored. The Internet acts as a Research Lab in every city of yours on its continent. Build it on your main landmass to raise research across your core cities.
buildings.civilDefense: Air-raid shelters, sirens and fire brigades protected civilians in wartime. Civil Defense strengthens the city's defenders by half against bombardment and air attack. It requires Barracks; build it in front-line cities that are exposed to enemy artillery, bombers or naval guns.
buildings.stockExchange: Exchanges let companies raise capital by selling shares to the public. A Stock Exchange adds another half to the city's tax output on top of the Bank it requires. Build it in your richest cities; it is also needed before Wall Street.
buildings.commercialDock: Container ports and shipping terminals came to handle most of the world's trade. A Commercial Dock adds one commerce to every water tile the city works that already yields commerce, though it pollutes a little. It requires a Harbor and turns coastal cities into strong earners.
buildings.templeOfArtemis: The temple to Artemis at Ephesus was famed for its size and its forest of marble columns. The Temple of Artemis acts as a Temple in every city of yours on its continent, making an unhappy citizen content in each. It loses its effect with Education.
buildings.statueOfZeus: A huge seated figure of Zeus in gold and ivory stood in the temple at Olympia. The Statue of Zeus requires Ivory and provides a free [Ancient Cavalry](pedia:units/ancientCavalry) unit in its city every five turns until Metallurgy makes it obsolete. It gives an early military civilization a steady flow of mounted troops.
buildings.mausoleumOfMausollos: The tomb of a Carian ruler was so grand that his name became the word for any monumental tomb. The Mausoleum of Mausollos makes three unhappy citizens content in its own city. It is a good way to steady a growing capital in the ancient era.
buildings.knightsTemplar: The Knights Templar were a military order founded to protect pilgrims on the road to Jerusalem. Knights Templar produces a free [Crusader](pedia:units/crusader) in its city every five turns until Steam Power makes it obsolete. It suits a civilization that means to fight its way through the Middle Ages.
buildings.secretPoliceHq: Feared state security services enforced loyalty under authoritarian regimes. The Secret Police HQ can only be built under [Communism](pedia:governments/communism), where it serves as a secondary seat of government for [corruption](pedia:concepts/corruption). Place it in a distant region of your empire.

governments.anarchy: When a government falls, no one is fully in charge until a new order takes hold. Anarchy is the interval of a few turns between governments: there is no research, all commerce goes to luxury, corruption is catastrophic, and any tile yielding more than two food, shields or commerce loses one. Buildings cost no upkeep and there is no war weariness, but production cannot be hurried, no one can be drafted and no units are supported for free. Keep revolutions rare.
governments.despotism: The first states were ruled by a single strongman whose word was law. Under Despotism corruption is rampant, and any tile producing more than two food, shields or commerce loses one unless the city is celebrating. Each city supports a few units for free, troops in a city keep order as military police, and production is hurried by sacrificing citizens. Once [Nationalism](pedia:techs/nationalism) is known, each city may draft up to 2 units a turn. There is no war weariness. Leave it as soon as a better government is available.
governments.monarchy: Hereditary kings ruled most of the world's great states for thousands of years. Monarchy lifts the Despotism tile penalty and lowers corruption to a problematic level. Larger cities support more free units, troops keep order in their city, production is hurried with gold, and with [Nationalism](pedia:techs/nationalism) each city may draft up to 2 units a turn. With no war weariness at all, it is a steady choice for an expanding empire that expects to fight.
governments.communism: Communist states placed the whole economy under central planning by the party. Under Communism corruption is the same moderate share in every city regardless of distance, with none in the capital, which favours sprawling empires. Every city supports several units for free, troops keep order, and production is hurried with forced labour; with [Nationalism](pedia:techs/nationalism) each city may also draft up to 2 units a turn. There is no war weariness, and only a Communist state can build the [Secret Police HQ](pedia:buildings/secretPoliceHq).
governments.republic: Republics from ancient Rome to the merchant cities of Italy placed power in elected councils. A Republic adds one commerce to every tile that already yields commerce and keeps corruption at a nuisance level. Few units are supported for free and each extra unit costs two gold; troops do not keep order, war weariness is low, production is hurried with gold, and a city may draft only 1 unit a turn. It is the strongest economy for a mostly peaceful civilization.
governments.democracy: Modern democracies answer to voters through free elections and a free press. Democracy adds one commerce to tiles that already yield commerce, keeps corruption minimal and independent of distance from the capital, and its workers work faster. No units are supported for free, troops do not keep order and war weariness is high, so long wars quickly breed unrest. Production is hurried with gold, and a city may draft only 1 unit a turn. Choose it for peaceful economic and scientific growth.
governments.fascism: Fascist regimes of the twentieth century fused nationalism, militarism and the cult of a leader. Fascism keeps corruption at a nuisance level, gives workers the fastest work rate of any government and supports more free units than any other, especially in large cities. Production is hurried with forced labour, each city may draft up to 2 units a turn, troops keep order and there is no war weariness. It is a government built for total war, at the cost of the commerce bonus enjoyed by free societies.
governments.feudalism: Feudal societies bound lords and vassals through oaths of service in exchange for land. Feudalism shares Monarchy's level of corruption but hurries production with forced labour, and with [Nationalism](pedia:techs/nationalism) each city may draft up to 2 units a turn. It supports many free units in small towns and few in large cities, and each unit beyond that costs three gold. Troops keep order and war weariness is low. It suits a wide empire of small towns defended by many inexpensive units.

specialists.laborer: Most citizens of a city work the fields, mines and waters around it. A laborer works one tile in the city's work area and brings in its food, shields and commerce. Laborers are the only citizens with a mood, so they decide whether a city is content, celebrating or in [disorder](pedia:concepts/happiness).
specialists.entertainer: Musicians, actors and street performers have always lifted the spirits of a crowd. An Entertainer works no tile but adds luxury, which makes citizens happy or content. Cities turn laborers into entertainers to avoid disorder, and you can assign them yourself when a city has more people than good tiles.
specialists.taxCollector: Collecting revenue efficiently has always been central to running a state. A Tax Collector works no tile but adds gold to the city's tax income, which Marketplaces and Banks then multiply. Use them in cities that have outgrown their useful tiles when your treasury runs short.
specialists.scientist: Scholars and researchers push back the boundaries of knowledge. A Scientist works no tile but adds beakers to the city's [science](pedia:concepts/science), which Libraries and Universities then multiply. Assign them in cities with spare citizens when you are racing for an advance.
specialists.policeman: Professional police help keep local officials honest and the streets orderly. A Policeman works no tile but reduces corruption and waste in the city. They become available with [Nationalism](pedia:techs/nationalism) and suit distant cities that lose much of their output.
specialists.civilEngineer: Engineers plan and oversee construction projects of every kind. A Civil Engineer works no tile but adds shields toward buildings and wonders, though not toward units. Available from [Replaceable Parts](pedia:techs/replaceableParts), they help cities with spare citizens finish improvements faster.
